kill_argument: The literature record now checks out, but it still lets the plan state the IV interpretation more firmly than its sources allow. The contribution conditions the 'positively weighted average of returns for men whose schooling responds to proximity' reading on monotonicity and rich covariates. It reports only the rejection of rich covariates. It omits that Tuebbicke, already in the bibliography, reports defiers evidence on these data: the reordered instrument halves 2SLS from 0.570 to 0.289. It also cites Angrist-Imbens for conditions its recorded abstract never states. H5 still asserts the unconditional reading. The new exclusion claim repeats Jiang et al.'s 'statistically significant' although their own triply robust interval, (-0.01, 0.23), includes zero. All of this is wording. What I tried and it held: Tuebbicke Table 3 and p. 2990; the Card (2000) reference list (OCR); the TP 127 abstract (OCR); Jiang Table 3; Luo Table 2; GKM19 Table 3 critical values and its homoskedasticity statements (pp. 489-490); the GKM24 abstract; the Londschien-Buehlmann heteroskedasticity caveat; the ASS projection and Lee non-extension (manuscript sec. 5); Sun 2018 project() and Table 2; the ivmodels API. The hedged novelty claim stands; I found only course handouts computing an effective F with nearc4.

findings.text: The interpretation the plan adopts is contradicted by a verified source in its own bibliography and is not supported by a fetched source in the form stated. plan.json contribution: 'interprets the IV estimate as a weighted average of returns for men whose schooling responds to proximity'; H5: 'Under the heterogeneous-returns reading the paper adopts, a difference would compare a weighted average of returns for men whose schooling responds to proximity'. (a) Blandhol et al. (blandhol2025tsls, sec. 6.1 and Table 3, which I read in WP 29709) show that with Card's additive, non-saturated covariates TSLS is 'weakly causal' only under rich covariates. Their RESET test rejects that condition on Card's data (p = 0.000), and their LATE/ACR estimates are 0.067 (DDML) and 0.085 (IPSW) against TSLS 0.132. Claim c-bbmt-card records this, but the plan's interpretation sentence ignores it. Sources notes sec. 5 item 9 mentions it only as 'may not even be a positively weighted LATE'. (b) Kling (kling2001interpreting, WP p. 6) states the weighted-average reading 'conditional on X' under his model's assumptions. Card (fn. 10) cites Angrist and Imbens (1993), which the Scout lists as unverified. No citation claim records the reading with its conditions. (c) Missing: Tuebbicke (2023), 'When to use matching and weighting or regression in instrumental variable estimation? Evidence from college proximity and returns to college', Empirical Economics 65, DOI 10.1007/s00181-023-02441-7 (Crossref abstract read). On Card's data it finds 2SLS 50-100% larger than instrument-propensity-score estimators, because of conditional-variance weighting. Sloczynski (2021, IZA DP 14349) is the theory behind it and is also unfetched. Since the seed requirement turns on how the IV estimate is described, the paper would print an interpretation that its own literature says fails on these data.
findings.evidence: plan.json contribution (last sentence) and hypotheses H5 (last sentence); claims.jsonl c-bbmt-card (no claim for the weighted-average reading); sources/notes.md sec. 5 item 9 and sec. 3 'Not verified' list (Angrist and Imbens, Sloczynski 2021); refs.bib (no Tuebbicke, no Angrist-Imbens).
findings.response: Fixed by the PI: H5's last sentence now carries the contribution's qualifier; design.estimand was already qualified by the Designer.
findings.ruling: Mostly fixed, one named sentence not. Fixed: plan.json contribution now gives the conditional reading (monotonicity and rich covariates), says Blandhol et al. reject rich covariates for Panel A col 5 and cites Tuebbicke. c-kling-weighted matches Kling (WP p. 4; notes sec. 3 quote). tubbicke2023when and angrist1995twostage are recorded; I checked Tuebbicke Table 3 (journal p. 2989) and the TP 127 abstract (OCR), and both match c-tubbicke and c-angrist-imbens. Still open: the last sentence of H5, which the r1 evidence named, is unchanged: 'Under the heterogeneous-returns reading the paper adopts, a difference would compare a weighted average of returns for men whose schooling responds to proximity with an OLS coefficient'. That contradicts the contribution's 'on these data even that reading is not guaranteed'. design.estimand has the same unconditional sentence ('under heterogeneous returns this is a weighted average of returns for men whose schooling responds to proximity'); that one is for the design review. Downgraded from major to minor: the sentence that states the paper's interpretation is now correctly qualified, and what remains is a one-clause inconsistency. The fix is to copy the contribution's qualifier into H5 (and into design.estimand).
findings.remedy: Cheapest fix is to narrow the wording, with no new analysis. Read the estimand as 'under monotonicity and correctly specified (rich) covariates, a positively weighted average of returns for men whose schooling responds to proximity'. Then state that Blandhol et al.'s RESET test rejects rich covariates for Card's Panel A column 5, so not even that reading is guaranteed. Add a citation claim for Kling's 'conditional on X' sentence. Have the Scout fetch and record Tuebbicke (2023) and Angrist and Imbens (1995, JASA) before either is cited, or drop the Angrist-Imbens attribution.

findings.text: The published chapter's tables are still unverified, and there is cheap evidence on both sides. Kling (WP 7989, Table 1, p. 20) labels his replicated columns 'Card (1995b): T2-c2' (OLS .073 (.003)) and 'T3-c5B' (IV .132 (.049)) and gives the chapter as pp. 201-221. In WP 4483, Table 2 col 2 is 0.075 (0.003) and Table 3 Panel B col 5 is 0.122 (0.046). So the chapter's column numbering, and possibly its OLS standard error, may differ from the WP's. The Scout reads Kling's labels as his own error (notes sec. 3), which the files cannot settle. Card (2001), 'Estimating the Return to Schooling: Progress on Some Persistent Econometric Problems' (NBER WP 7769, Table II row 4; I read it), cites 'Card (1995b)' with OLS 0.073 (0.004), IV 0.132 (0.049) and the interaction-instrument IV 0.097 (0.048). That confirms the chapter's headline numbers equal the WP's but says nothing on the Panel A columns or numbering. The bibliography lacks Card (2001). The card1995chapter record's method, 'fetched-catalogue-record', is not one of the three methods PROTOCOL.md defines, and the validator does not catch it.
findings.evidence: sources/sources.json card1995chapter (method, note); sources/notes.md sec. 0 and sec. 3 Kling row; refs.bib card1995chapter pages 201--222.
findings.response: Scout: recorded Card (2000, NBER WP 7769; Table 2 row 4 confirms 0.073 (0.004), 0.132 (0.049), 0.097 (0.048); ref list gives pp. 201-222); dropped card1995chapter from refs.bib/sources.json since no protocol method fits; notes sec. 0 states the chapter's tables were not seen, records Kling's differing labels as unresolved, and asks for 'WP 4483 Table x, Panel y, column z' labels.
findings.ruling: card1995chapter is dropped from refs.bib and sources.json, so no non-protocol method remains. card2000estimating is recorded. I checked its reference list (WP 7769 printed p. 40, OCR): 'Aspects of Labour Market Behaviour ... (University of Toronto Press, Toronto): 201-222'. Table 2 row 4 I had checked in r1. notes sec. 0 tells the paper to label targets as WP 4483 columns, to say the chapter's tables were not seen, and to leave Kling's labels unresolved. c-card-wp-citation and c-card2000-headline say no more than this.
findings.remedy: Record Card (2001) as a verified source supporting the chapter's headline numbers. In the paper, label every target as 'WP 4483 Table x, Panel y, column z' and state that the chapter's tables were not seen, that Kling's column labels differ, and that Card's OLS SE (0.004) is the target. Use one of the protocol's method values for card1995chapter, or have the protocol define the extra value.

findings.text: Three citation claims say more than, or something other than, their sources. (a) c-validity-tests cites kitagawa2015test, whose record is abstract-only and whose abstract does not mention Card. The Kitagawa result is known only through Carr and Kitagawa (sec. 5.1). That source also says Kitagawa (2015) conditioned on up to five covariates, and that both tests binarise education at 16+ years, which can itself violate exclusion through coarsening bias. The claim and notes sec. 5 item 2 use this test to favour Panel A col 6 ('full covariate set') without saying that it tests a binarised-treatment model. (b) c-bbmt-card says 'reproduce Card's IV estimate' but the estimate is Panel A column 5 (Blandhol et al. call it Card's 'main results'), not the basic Panel B col 6 estimate that also prints 0.132. (c) c-ivmodel-card calls the Kang et al. AR interval 'homoskedastic'. The paper's code uses the default homoskedastic model, but the paper does not label the interval that way (sec. 3.3 offers a heteroskedastic variant). Say 'computed under the default homoskedastic model'.
findings.evidence: claims.jsonl c-validity-tests, c-bbmt-card, c-ivmodel-card; sources/sources.json kitagawa2015test ('Abstract page only'); sources/notes.md sec. 3 Kitagawa row and sec. 5 item 2.
findings.response: Scout: c-validity-tests now rests on carr2021testing only, attributes Kitagawa's result to Carr-Kitagawa and adds the 16+-year binarisation and coarsening-bias caveat; c-bbmt-card names Panel A column 5; c-ivmodel-card says 'computed under the package's default homoskedastic model'; notes sec. 3 and sec. 5 item 2 updated.
findings.ruling: c-validity-tests now rests on carr2021testing alone, attributes Kitagawa's result to Carr and Kitagawa, and carries the 16+-year binarisation and coarsening-bias caveat. c-bbmt-card names Panel A column 5. c-ivmodel-card says 'computed under the package's default homoskedastic model'. notes sec. 5 item 2 now calls the support for col 6 'weak, indirect'.
findings.remedy: Support c-validity-tests with carr2021testing only, and attribute the Kitagawa result as 'reported by Carr and Kitagawa'. Add 'with education binarised at 16 or more years'. Name Panel A column 5 in c-bbmt-card. Qualify 'homoskedastic' in c-ivmodel-card.

findings.text: There is an obvious, though not novelty-threatening, gap in the record of exclusion-restriction work on these data. Luo, Li, Miao and He (arXiv 2206.08228, sec. 6, Table 2; I read it) reanalyse Card's 3,010 men without imposing exclusion. They use a binary post-high-school treatment and negative controls, and find 'no significant evidence of violating the exclusion restriction'. They cite earlier analyses of the same data by Tan (2006), Kedagni (2021) and Jiang et al. (2022). Tuebbicke (2023) (see L1) is a further reanalysis. Card's own survey (Card 2001, see L2) is the standard place where the proximity estimate is set against other IV estimates. None of these changes the narrow contribution, which is a robust AR, effective F and CHR breakdown on Panel A col 6, and I found none reporting those. But a paper that discusses 'what would violate' exclusion should not present Cinelli-Hazlett and Steiner et al. as the whole exclusion-sensitivity literature on these data.
findings.evidence: sources/notes.md sec. 3 (table of reanalyses) and sec. 6 (novelty verdict); refs.bib.
findings.response: Scout: fetched and recorded Luo et al. (2024, arXiv v2 Table 2) and Jiang, Yang and Ding (2022, arXiv v2 Table 3), plus Tübbicke 2023 and Card 2000; claim c-principal-strata; notes sec. 3 labels the reanalysis table a selection and lists Tan 2006 and Kédagni 2021 as not fetched.
findings.ruling: luo2024identification and jiang2022multiply are fetched and recorded. notes sec. 3 calls the reanalysis table 'a selection' and lists Tan and Kedagni as not fetched. The wording of the new claim built on these two sources is a separate problem; see L6.
findings.remedy: Either have the Scout fetch and record Luo et al. (2022) and one of Tan/Kedagni/Jiang et al., or have the paper describe its list of reanalyses as a selection and not cite these works. No change to the hypotheses.

findings.text: The plan cites a monotonicity condition but not the evidence against it in its own bibliography, and it cites Angrist and Imbens for more than the recorded text says. (a) plan.json contribution: 'under monotonicity and correctly specified (rich) covariates it would be a positively weighted average ... but Blandhol et al. (2025) reject the rich-covariates condition ... and Tubbicke (2023) finds 2SLS well above estimators that do not rely on it'. Only the covariate condition is said to be in doubt. Tuebbicke (journal p. 2990, Table 3 Panel C), which the bibliography holds, reports that Sloczynski (2021) attributes the large 2SLS estimate to defiers. With his reordered instrument, the saturated-specification 2SLS falls from 0.570 to 0.289. sloczynski2024abadie (c-sloczynski) also names failures of monotonicity. c-tubbicke records only the conditional-variance-weighting result, and notes sec. 3 calls Sloczynski (2021) 'the theory' for that result alone. (b) The contribution also omits that Tuebbicke's comparison uses a binary 'some college' treatment on n = 2,988 with no family background. That is a different estimand from Card's years-of-schooling 2SLS, so 'finds 2SLS well above' is evidence by analogy. (c) The contribution cites '(Angrist and Imbens 1995; Kling 2001)' for a reading conditioned on monotonicity, covariates and men whose schooling responds. The only Angrist-Imbens text read is the 1992 TP 127 abstract (I OCR'd it): 'given mild regularity assumptions, instrumental variables independence assumptions identify a weighted average of per-unit causal effects ... Conventional instrumental variables and Two-Stage Least Squares procedures can be interpreted as estimating the average causal response'. It names no monotonicity condition, no covariate condition and no complier population. c-angrist-imbens correctly says only that. The conditions rest on Kling alone.
findings.evidence: plan.json contribution (last two sentences); claims.jsonl c-tubbicke, c-angrist-imbens, c-sloczynski; sources/notes.md sec. 3 Tuebbicke row; Tuebbicke (2023) journal pp. 2989-2990, Table 3 Panels B-C; NBER TP 127 abstract.
findings.response: Scout: c-tubbicke now states the binary 'some college' estimand (n = 2,988, no family background) and adds the Sloczynski/defier result (saturated 2SLS 0.570 -> 0.289 with the reordered instrument); c-angrist-imbens now says the recorded abstract names no monotonicity, covariate or complier condition; notes sec. 3 (Kling, Kitagawa, Tubbicke rows) and sec. 5 item 9 attribute the conditional wording to Kling only and record that monotonicity is questioned. plan.json left to the PI. PI (plan.json): contribution now names the monotonicity doubt (Tubbicke citing Sloczynski, 0.570 to 0.289), Tubbicke's different estimand and n, and limits Angrist-Imbens to the general reading.
findings.remedy: Wording only. Add to c-tubbicke: 'and, reporting Sloczynski (2021), that accounting for defiers with a reordered instrument lowers the saturated 2SLS estimate from 0.570 to 0.289'. Add to the contribution that monotonicity is also questioned on these data (Tuebbicke, reporting Sloczynski; Sloczynski, Uysal and Wooldridge), and that Tuebbicke's evidence concerns a binary 'some college' treatment. Cite Angrist and Imbens only for the general average-causal-response reading, and Kling for the conditional, complier-weighted wording. Fetch Sloczynski (2021) only if the paper will cite it directly.

findings.text: c-principal-strata repeats the authors' prose where their own tables are weaker. The claim says the analyses 'find no significant evidence that college proximity affects log wages other than through education, and a positive effect of education on earnings (Jiang, Yang and Ding 2022; Luo, Li, Miao and He 2024)'. (a) Jiang et al. (arXiv v2 sec. 6.1, p. 20) write 'The estimated tau10 is positive and statistically significant'. But their Table 3 (p. 22) gives the triply robust estimate as 0.10 (-0.01, 0.23), an interval that includes 0, and their unstabilised weighting estimator gives -0.87 (-1.69, -0.05). Only the regression and stabilised-weighting estimators exclude 0. (b) Luo et al. (arXiv v2 Table 2, p. 14): in the preferred case (iv) the complier effect is 0.85 (0.00, 1.88), with its lower bound at 0. Cases (i)-(ii), which the authors discount as misspecified, give significantly negative effects for compliers and for the never-taker stratum: case (i) Delta_ss-bar -0.68 (-1.85, -0.25) and Delta_s-bar-s-bar -0.86 (-2.83, -0.32). A significantly non-zero never-taker effect is a direct effect of proximity. (c) Both papers estimate the effect of a binary 'beyond high school' indicator; Luo's 0.85 log points is not on Card's per-year scale. notes sec. 3 records the intervals correctly and calls the evidence 'weak', but the claim, which is what the paper will cite, does not.
findings.evidence: claims.jsonl c-principal-strata; sources/notes.md sec. 3 Jiang and Luo rows; Jiang, Yang and Ding arXiv v2 p. 20 text vs Table 3 p. 22; Luo et al. arXiv v2 Table 2 p. 14 and the text below it.
findings.response: Scout: c-principal-strata narrowed to the tables: no significant direct effect for always/never-takers in preferred specifications, imprecise complier effects on a binary 'beyond high school' scale (Jiang et al. TR 0.10 (-0.01, 0.23); Luo et al. 0.85 (0.00, 1.88)), and Luo et al.'s case (i) never-taker effect -0.86 (-2.83, -0.32); 'positive effect of education' dropped; notes Jiang and Luo rows updated.
findings.remedy: Narrow the claim: 'In their preferred specifications, principal-stratification reanalyses that drop the exclusion restriction (binary treatment: schooling beyond high school) find no significant direct effect of proximity for always- and never-takers; their complier estimates are imprecise (Jiang et al.'s triply robust interval includes 0)'. Drop 'a positive effect of education on earnings', or attribute it to the authors with the interval.
